module.title: Electrochemistry & Corrosion
module.intro: Electrochemistry sits at the boundary between thermodynamics and kinetics, linking chemical energy to electrical energy through the transfer of electrons. This module builds the theory from the half-cell up: standard potentials and the Nernst equation establish what is thermodynamically possible, Butler-Volmer kinetics governs how fast it happens, and Pourbaix diagrams map the conditions under which metals corrode. The final articles apply these ideas to the real problems of corrosion engineering and energy storage.

articles.title: Electrochemical Cells & Standard Potentials
articles.description: Half-cells, the standard hydrogen electrode, cell EMF, the electrochemical series, and the link between free energy and voltage.
articles.intro: Every electrochemical cell is built from two half-reactions. Understanding how to split a reaction into its electrode components, assign potentials, and calculate the driving force for electron transfer is the foundation of everything that follows in this module.
body: Electrons must flow through a wire
Consider zinc metal placed in a solution of copper sulphate. Zinc dissolves and copper plates out. The net reaction is:

This is a redox reaction. Zinc is oxidised (loses electrons), copper is reduced (gains them). If the two metals are in the same beaker, the electron transfer happens at the zinc surface and all the chemical energy is released as heat. Useful for a lecture demonstration, useless for doing work.

Separate the reactants. Put the zinc in one beaker of ZnSO$_4$ solution and the copper in another beaker of CuSO$_4$ solution. Connect the metals by a wire and the solutions by a salt bridge. Now the electrons must travel through the external circuit to get from zinc to copper. That flow of electrons is an electrical current, and you can use it to do work. This is a galvanic cell.
Every electrochemical cell consists of two half-reactions. For the Daniell cell above:

Oxidation always occurs at the anode. Reduction always occurs at the cathode. This is true for galvanic cells (which produce electricity) and electrolytic cells (which consume it). The only difference is the sign of the cell voltage and whether the process is spontaneous.
Oxidation at the Anode: both start with vowels. Reduction at the Cathode: both start with consonants. Simple enough that you should never need to look it up again.

You cannot measure the absolute potential of a single half-cell. Voltage is always a difference. You need a reference electrode. By international convention, the reference is the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE):

This half-reaction is assigned a potential of exactly 0.000 V at all temperatures. Every other standard electrode potential $E^\circ$ is measured relative to this. The SHE uses a platinised platinum electrode in 1 mol/L HCl with hydrogen gas bubbled over it at 1 bar. It is not the most convenient electrode in practice (the Ag/AgCl and saturated calomel electrodes are far more common in the lab), but it is the universal reference point.
Measuring each half-reaction against the SHE produces a table of standard reduction potentials $E^\circ$. Some representative values at 298 K:

The series orders metals by their tendency to lose electrons. Metals with large negative $E^\circ$ are strong reducing agents (they corrode easily). Metals with large positive $E^\circ$ are noble (they resist oxidation). This is why gold survives millennia in seawater while iron rusts in months.
The electromotive force (EMF) of a cell is the potential difference between cathode and anode under zero-current conditions:
For the Daniell cell: $E_{\text{cell}} = +0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10$ V. A positive cell EMF means the reaction is spontaneous as written.

The connection to thermodynamics is direct. When $n$ moles of electrons pass through a potential difference $E$, the electrical work done is $nFE$, where $F = 96\,485$ C/mol is the Faraday constant. At constant temperature and pressure, the maximum non-expansion work equals $-\Delta G$. Therefore:

For the Daniell cell: $\Delta G = -2 \times 96\,485 \times 1.10 = -212\,267$ J/mol $\approx -212$ kJ/mol. The large negative value confirms a strong thermodynamic driving force. Under standard conditions:
The link between $\Delta G$ and $E$ follows from equating the electrical work to the Gibbs free energy change for a reversible process.

For a reversible electrochemical cell operating at constant $T$ and $P$, the only non-PV work is electrical work. The first law gives $dU = \delta Q + \delta W_{PV} + \delta W_{\text{elec}}$. For a reversible process at constant $P$: $dH = \delta Q + \delta W_{\text{elec}}$, and at constant $T$: $dG = dH - TdS = \delta Q - TdS + \delta W_{\text{elec}}$. For a reversible process, $\delta Q = TdS$, so:

The electrical work done on the system when charge $dq = nF$ flows through potential $E$ is $\delta W_{\text{elec}} = -nFE$ (negative because the cell does work on the external circuit). Therefore $\Delta G = -nFE$. This is exact for a reversible cell, and it provides the upper bound on the work obtainable from any real cell.
In a galvanic cell, the reaction is spontaneous ($\Delta G < 0$, $E > 0$). The cell produces electrical energy. Batteries are galvanic cells.

In an electrolytic cell, an external voltage is applied to drive a non-spontaneous reaction ($\Delta G > 0$). Electrolysis of water, electroplating, and aluminium smelting (the Hall-Heroult process, which runs at about 4 V and consumes roughly 13 kWh per kg of aluminium produced) are all electrolytic processes.
The same cell can operate in either mode. A rechargeable battery is galvanic during discharge and electrolytic during charge.
The conventional shorthand for a cell writes the anode on the left and the cathode on the right, with single vertical lines for phase boundaries and a double vertical line for the salt bridge:

This notation encodes all the information needed to write the half-reactions and calculate $E_{\text{cell}}$. The rule: the right-hand electrode is always the cathode (reduction), and the cell EMF is positive if the overall reaction is spontaneous.
A cell is constructed from a standard silver electrode and a standard zinc electrode. Write the cell notation, the half-reactions, and calculate $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$ and $\Delta G^\circ$.
Zinc has the more negative standard potential ($-0.76$ V), so it is the anode. Silver ($+0.80$ V) is the cathode.
The large positive EMF and large negative $\Delta G^\circ$ confirm a strongly spontaneous reaction. This is consistent with the large separation in the electrochemical series.

articles.title: The Nernst Equation
articles.description: How cell potential depends on concentration and temperature, the meaning of the reaction quotient, and the connection to equilibrium constants.
articles.intro: Standard potentials apply at unit activity. Real electrochemical cells almost never operate at unit activity. The Nernst equation tells you how the cell potential shifts with concentration, temperature, and pressure. It is the single most important quantitative tool in electrochemistry.
body: From free energy to the Nernst equation
We showed in article 10.1 that $\Delta G = -nFE$. From thermodynamics, the free energy change for a reaction at arbitrary activities is:

where $Q$ is the reaction quotient, the ratio of product activities to reactant activities each raised to their stoichiometric powers. Substituting $\Delta G = -nFE$ and $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$:
This is the Nernst equation. At 298.15 K, converting to base-10 logarithms ($\ln Q = 2.303 \log Q$):
The factor $RT/F = 0.02569$ V at 298 K is the thermal voltage. It sets the scale: each tenfold change in the activity ratio shifts the potential by $59.16/n$ mV.

Pure solids have unit activity by convention, so Zn(s) and Cu(s) do not appear. For dilute solutions, activity $\approx$ concentration in mol/L. If $[\text{Zn}^{2+}] = 0.01$ M and $[\text{Cu}^{2+}] = 1.0$ M:
The cell potential increases because we have diluted the product and concentrated the reactant. Le Chatelier in action.

A concentration cell uses the same electrode material on both sides, with different electrolyte concentrations. The standard potentials cancel, and the EMF arises purely from the concentration difference.
Consider two copper electrodes, one in 0.001 M CuSO$_4$ and the other in 1.0 M CuSO$_4$:

89 mV from a concentration ratio alone. Copper dissolves from the dilute side and plates out on the concentrated side, driving the system toward equal concentrations. This is thermodynamics enforcing equilibrium.

Concentration cells are not just curiosities. The oxygen concentration cell is the mechanism behind crevice corrosion: different oxygen concentrations on either side of a crevice create a potential difference that drives metal dissolution (article 10.5).
The Nernst equation contains $T$ explicitly. The temperature coefficient of the cell EMF is:

This follows from $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ and $\Delta G = -nFE$. If $\Delta S > 0$ (the reaction produces more disorder), the cell potential increases with temperature. If $\Delta S < 0$, it decreases.

For the hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, $\Delta S < 0$ (two gases combine to form a liquid), so the open-circuit voltage falls with temperature. At 298 K it is 1.229 V; at 353 K (80 $^\circ$C, typical PEM operating temperature) it drops to about 1.18 V.
At equilibrium, $\Delta G = 0$, which means $E = 0$ and $Q = K$ (the equilibrium constant). The Nernst equation becomes:
This provides a powerful way to measure equilibrium constants. A cell with $E^\circ = +1.10$ V and $n = 2$ gives:
An astronomically large equilibrium constant. The reaction goes essentially to completion. Even modest cell voltages correspond to enormous equilibrium constants because $F$ is such a large number.

The Faraday constant $F = 96\,485$ C/mol is Avogadro's number times the elementary charge. It converts between moles and coulombs. Because $F$ is nearly $10^5$, even a 1 V cell potential corresponds to $\sim$100 kJ/mol of free energy, enough to shift equilibrium constants by tens of orders of magnitude. This is why electrochemistry is so effective at driving reactions.

In dilute solutions, activity $\approx$ molarity. In concentrated electrolytes, this breaks down. The activity of an ion is $a_i = \gamma_i m_i$, where $\gamma_i$ is the activity coefficient and $m_i$ is the molality. For strong electrolytes at moderate concentration, $\gamma < 1$ because ion-ion interactions stabilise the solute. Debye-Huckel theory gives $\log \gamma_\pm = -A|z_+z_-|\sqrt{I}$ for the mean activity coefficient at low ionic strength $I$, where $A = 0.509$ (mol/kg)$^{-1/2}$ in water at 298 K.

For a 0.1 mol/kg solution of CuSO$_4$ ($z_+ = 2$, $z_- = 2$, $I = 0.4$ mol/kg): $\log \gamma_\pm \approx -0.509 \times 4 \times \sqrt{0.4} \approx -1.29$, giving $\gamma_\pm \approx 0.051$. The effective activity is 20 times lower than the nominal concentration. Ignoring activity coefficients in concentrated solutions leads to significant errors in the Nernst equation.
A hydrogen electrode operates at pH 7 (i.e., $a_{\text{H}^+} = 10^{-7}$) with $P_{\text{H}_2} = 1$ bar. Calculate its potential versus SHE at 298 K.

At neutral pH, the hydrogen electrode sits at $-0.414$ V vs SHE. This is the potential of the lower boundary in the Pourbaix diagram for water at pH 7 (article 10.4). Every 59.2 mV per pH unit is a useful number to remember: it appears everywhere in corrosion science.

articles.title: Electrode Kinetics & Butler-Volmer
articles.description: Overpotential, exchange current density, the Butler-Volmer equation, Tafel slopes, and the limiting cases that govern real electrode behaviour.
articles.intro: The Nernst equation tells you where equilibrium lies. It says nothing about how fast you get there. Electrode kinetics governs the rate of electron transfer at an interface, and the Butler-Volmer equation is its central result. Understanding it is essential for predicting corrosion rates, designing batteries, and optimising electrolysis.
body: Apply a potential to an electrode and measure the current. At the equilibrium potential $E_{\text{eq}}$ (given by the Nernst equation), no net current flows. The forward and reverse reactions proceed at equal rates. Shift the potential away from equilibrium, and one direction is favoured. The deviation from equilibrium is the overpotential:

A positive $\eta$ (anodic overpotential) drives oxidation. A negative $\eta$ (cathodic overpotential) drives reduction. The overpotential is the driving force for net electrochemical reaction, analogous to how undercooling drives solidification or how supersaturation drives precipitation.

Overpotential is not a single phenomenon. It has contributions from charge transfer at the electrode surface (activation overpotential), from concentration gradients in the electrolyte (concentration overpotential), and from resistive losses in the electrolyte and connections (ohmic overpotential, or $iR$ drop). The Butler-Volmer equation describes the first of these.

At equilibrium, the electrode is not static. Atoms are continuously oxidising and reducing at the surface, but the two rates are equal. The current density corresponding to this dynamic equilibrium is the exchange current density $j_0$. It is a measure of how kinetically facile the electrode reaction is.
H$_2$ evolution on Pt: $j_0 \approx 10^{-3}$ A/cm$^2$ (fast, platinum is an excellent catalyst)
H$_2$ evolution on Hg: $j_0 \approx 10^{-12}$ A/cm$^2$ (extremely slow, high overpotential needed)

The nine orders of magnitude separating hydrogen evolution on platinum from hydrogen evolution on mercury explain why mercury was historically used as a cathode in the chlor-alkali process: the high overpotential for H$_2$ evolution suppresses this unwanted side reaction, allowing chlorine to be produced instead.

Consider a single-step electron transfer at an electrode. The forward (anodic, oxidation) rate increases exponentially with positive overpotential, and the reverse (cathodic, reduction) rate increases exponentially with negative overpotential. The net current density is their difference:

This is the Butler-Volmer equation. Here $\alpha_a$ and $\alpha_c$ are the anodic and cathodic transfer coefficients (for a single-step reaction, $\alpha_a + \alpha_c = 1$, and $\alpha_a = \alpha_c = 0.5$ is a common symmetric case). The equation has two parameters: $j_0$ (the magnitude) and $\alpha$ (the symmetry of the activation barrier).

The physical picture is an energy barrier at the electrode surface. The overpotential tilts the energy landscape. A fraction $\alpha_a$ of the applied overpotential lowers the barrier for the forward (anodic) direction, and a fraction $\alpha_c$ lowers it for the reverse.
The Butler-Volmer equation follows from transition state theory applied to the electrode-electrolyte interface.

The forward (anodic) rate constant is $k_a = k_a^0 \exp(\alpha_a F \eta / RT)$, and the reverse (cathodic) rate constant is $k_c = k_c^0 \exp(-\alpha_c F \eta / RT)$. At equilibrium ($\eta = 0$), the net rate is zero, so $k_a^0 c_{\text{Red}} = k_c^0 c_{\text{Ox}} = j_0 / F$. The net current density is:
j = F\left(k_a c_{\text{Red}} - k_c c_{\text{Ox}}\right) = j_0 \left[ \exp\left(\frac{\alpha_a F \eta}{RT}\right) - \exp\left(-\frac{\alpha_c F \eta}{RT}\right) \right]

The exponential terms are Boltzmann factors. The overpotential shifts the activation energy for the forward reaction by $-\alpha_a F \eta$ and for the reverse reaction by $+\alpha_c F \eta$, where $\alpha_a + \alpha_c = 1$ for a single electron transfer step.
At large overpotentials ($|\eta| \gg RT/F \approx 26$ mV at 298 K), one exponential dominates and the other is negligible. For anodic overpotentials:

This is the Tafel equation: a linear relationship between $\eta$ and $\log j$. The slope is the Tafel slope, $b = 2.303RT/(\alpha_a F)$. For $\alpha_a = 0.5$ at 298 K: $b = 2 \times 0.05916 / 1 = 118$ mV per decade of current. A slope of 120 mV/decade is the hallmark of a single-electron rate-determining step with a symmetric barrier.

Tafel plots ($\eta$ vs $\log j$) are the primary experimental tool for measuring $j_0$ and $\alpha$. Extrapolate the linear Tafel region back to $\eta = 0$; the intercept on the $\log j$ axis gives $\log j_0$.
At small overpotentials ($|\eta| \ll RT/F$), the exponentials can be linearised ($e^x \approx 1 + x$):
The electrode behaves as a resistor with a charge-transfer resistance:

This is directly measurable by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). For copper dissolution with $j_0 = 10^{-2}$ A/cm$^2$: $R_{\text{ct}} = 0.02569 / 10^{-2} = 2.6$ $\Omega$cm$^2$. For hydrogen evolution on mercury with $j_0 = 10^{-12}$ A/cm$^2$: $R_{\text{ct}} = 2.6 \times 10^{10}$ $\Omega$cm$^2$. The mercury electrode is effectively blocked.

At very high current densities, reactants are consumed at the electrode faster than diffusion can supply them. The surface concentration drops to zero, and the current saturates at the limiting current density:

where $D$ is the diffusion coefficient of the reacting species, $c_\infty$ is its bulk concentration, and $\delta$ is the diffusion layer thickness (typically 10-500 $\mu$m depending on stirring). For Cu$^{2+}$ in 0.1 M CuSO$_4$ with $D \approx 7 \times 10^{-6}$ cm$^2$/s and $\delta = 50$ $\mu$m:
Beyond this current density, the overpotential rises steeply (concentration overpotential) because the surface activity drops and the Nernst equation demands a large potential shift to compensate.

Every electrode has three kinetic regimes as overpotential increases: (1) linear ($j \propto \eta$) at small $\eta$, (2) Tafel ($\log j \propto \eta$) at moderate $\eta$, and (3) mass-transport limited ($j \to j_L$) at large $\eta$. A complete polarisation curve sweeps through all three. Knowing which regime your system operates in determines which parameter controls the rate.

The exchange current density for iron dissolution in 1 M H$_2$SO$_4$ is $j_0 = 10^{-5}$ A/cm$^2$ with $\alpha_a = 0.5$. Calculate the anodic current density at an overpotential of $\eta = +200$ mV at 298 K.
Since $\eta = 200$ mV $\gg 26$ mV, we are in the Tafel regime. The cathodic term is negligible:

The anodic current density is about 0.49 mA/cm$^2$, nearly 50 times the exchange current density. This corresponds to a corrosion rate of roughly 0.6 mm/year for iron (using Faraday's law: $\dot{m} = jM/(nF)$, then converting mass loss to penetration depth using $\rho_{\text{Fe}} = 7.87$ g/cm$^3$).

articles.title: Pourbaix Diagrams
articles.description: Potential-pH diagrams, the thermodynamic stability of metals in aqueous environments, and detailed construction of the iron Pourbaix diagram.
articles.intro: A Pourbaix diagram maps the thermodynamically stable species for a metal-water system as a function of electrode potential and pH. It is, in effect, a phase diagram for corrosion. Marcel Pourbaix published his Atlas of Electrochemical Equilibria in 1963, and these diagrams remain the starting point for any corrosion analysis.
body: An aqueous corrosion problem has two independent variables that matter most: the electrode potential (which controls the oxidation state of the metal) and the pH (which controls the concentration of H$^+$ and OH$^-$, and therefore the stability of oxides and hydroxides). A Pourbaix diagram plots potential on the vertical axis and pH on the horizontal axis, with lines separating regions where different species are thermodynamically stable.
Electrochemical equilibria involving electron transfer but no H$^+$ or OH$^-$: these give horizontal lines (potential-dependent, pH-independent).
Chemical equilibria involving H$^+$ or OH$^-$ but no electron transfer: these give vertical lines (pH-dependent, potential-independent).

Mixed equilibria involving both electrons and H$^+$/OH$^-$: these give sloping lines. The slope is always $-0.0592 \times (m/n)$ V per pH unit at 298 K, where $m$ is the number of H$^+$ involved and $n$ is the number of electrons.
Before drawing any metal boundaries, we need the stability limits of water itself. Two reactions define them.

Both lines have a slope of $-59.2$ mV per pH unit. Between them, water is thermodynamically stable. Above the upper line, water is oxidised to O$_2$. Below the lower line, water is reduced to H$_2$. Metals with equilibrium potentials below the lower line will spontaneously reduce water and corrode with hydrogen evolution, even in the absence of dissolved oxygen.
The iron Pourbaix diagram in detail

Iron is the most technologically important case. The key species are Fe (metal), Fe$^{2+}$ (ferrous ion), Fe$^{3+}$ (ferric ion), Fe$_2$O$_3$ (haematite, the stable oxide at high potentials), and Fe$_3$O$_4$ (magnetite, stable at intermediate potentials). Fe(OH)$_2$ also appears in some constructions, though it is metastable with respect to Fe$_3$O$_4$. We will work at 298 K with dissolved-ion activities of $10^{-6}$ M (a standard convention that represents dilute corrosion conditions).
Line 1: Fe/Fe$^{2+}$ equilibrium (horizontal, no pH dependence):
This horizontal line at $-0.617$ V separates metallic iron (below) from dissolved Fe$^{2+}$ (above). Below this potential, iron is immune to corrosion.

At $a_{\text{Fe}^{2+}} = 10^{-6}$: $E = 0.728 - 0.1776 \times \text{pH} + 0.355 = 1.083 - 0.1776 \times \text{pH}$. This line slopes downward to the right, separating dissolved Fe$^{2+}$ (below) from the protective Fe$_2$O$_3$ film (above). At pH 7, this gives $E \approx -0.16$ V.
Line 3: Fe$^{2+}$/Fe$^{3+}$ equilibrium (horizontal, no pH dependence):
At equal activities this is simply $E = +0.771$ V. This line only matters in the acidic region where both ions are in solution.
No electrons are transferred, so this boundary is a vertical line. At $a_{\text{Fe}^{3+}} = 10^{-6}$, the boundary falls at approximately pH 1.8.
The iron Pourbaix diagram divides into three types of region:
Immunity (bottom of diagram, low potentials): metallic iron is the stable phase. No corrosion occurs. This is the regime exploited by cathodic protection.

Corrosion (left and centre, where dissolved ions Fe$^{2+}$ or Fe$^{3+}$ are stable): iron dissolves. In acidic solutions at moderate potentials, Fe$^{2+}$ dominates. At higher potentials and low pH, Fe$^{3+}$ dominates.

Passivity (upper right, high potentials at moderate to high pH): solid oxides Fe$_2$O$_3$ or Fe$_3$O$_4$ are stable. These form a protective film on the surface. Stainless steels exploit this regime, where the chromium-enriched passive film is stable across a wide range of conditions.

For iron in aerated seawater (pH $\approx$ 8.1, dissolved O$_2$ setting the potential around +0.4 V vs SHE), the diagram places us squarely in the corrosion region where Fe$^{2+}$ is the stable dissolved species. This is why ships rust.
What Pourbaix diagrams do not tell you

A Pourbaix diagram is thermodynamic. It tells you what should happen, not how fast. Iron may sit in a "corrosion" region but corrode imperceptibly slowly because the kinetics are sluggish (high activation overpotential). Conversely, a metal in the "passivity" region may corrode rapidly if the passive film is mechanically damaged and cannot reform (erosion-corrosion). The diagram also assumes pure water as solvent; chloride ions, which are not shown, can break down passive films and shift the practical boundaries dramatically.

Aluminium: the passive region (Al$_2$O$_3$) spans pH 4 to 9. Below pH 4, aluminium dissolves as Al$^{3+}$. Above pH 9, it dissolves as aluminate Al(OH)$_4^-$. Aluminium is amphoteric: it corrodes in both strong acids and strong bases, but is protected in near-neutral water. This is why aluminium alloys perform well in atmospheric exposure but fail rapidly in contact with wet concrete (pH $\approx$ 13).

Copper: the immunity region extends above the hydrogen line. Copper does not corrode in de-aerated acid, because its equilibrium potential ($+0.34$ V) is above the hydrogen evolution potential. Dissolved oxygen or other oxidants are needed to drive copper corrosion. This is why copper water pipes last decades in most domestic supplies.

Titanium: the passive film (TiO$_2$) is stable across almost the entire Pourbaix diagram, from strongly acidic to strongly alkaline and from reducing to oxidising conditions. Only concentrated HF attacks titanium significantly. This extraordinary passivity explains its use in chemical process equipment, marine hardware, and biomedical implants.
Constructing Pourbaix lines from thermodynamic data
Each line on a Pourbaix diagram is a Nernst equation for a specific equilibrium, plotted as $E$ vs pH.
For a general half-reaction $a\text{Ox} + m\text{H}^+ + ne^- \rightleftharpoons b\text{Red} + c\text{H}_2\text{O}$, the Nernst equation is:

Since $\text{pH} = -\log a_{\text{H}^+}$, the $\text{H}^+$ term contributes $+(m/n) \times (RT \ln 10 / F) \times \text{pH}$ to $E^\circ$, giving a slope of $-0.0592(m/n)$ V per pH unit at 298 K. Set the dissolved ion activities to the chosen threshold (typically $10^{-6}$) and plot. Pure solids and water have unit activity.

Calculate the potential of the Fe/Fe$_3$O$_4$ boundary at pH 10, assuming $a_{\text{Fe}^{2+}} = 10^{-6}$ M. The relevant reaction is: $\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4 + 8\text{H}^+ + 8e^- \rightleftharpoons 3\text{Fe} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$, with $E^\circ = -0.085$ V.
For this reaction, $n = 8$ electrons and $m = 8$ protons. All solid phases have unit activity, so $Q = 1/(a_{\text{H}^+})^8$:

At pH 10, the Fe/Fe$_3$O$_4$ boundary lies at $-0.677$ V. This is well below the hydrogen evolution line at the same pH ($-0.592$ V), which means that in deaerated alkaline water, iron is close to the immunity region. In practice, alkaline environments (boiler water, for example) are much less corrosive to steel than neutral or acidic ones, consistent with this thermodynamic picture.

articles.title: Types of Corrosion
articles.description: Uniform corrosion, galvanic corrosion, pitting, crevice corrosion, intergranular corrosion, stress corrosion cracking, and erosion-corrosion: mechanisms, examples, and recognition.
articles.intro: Corrosion is electrochemistry happening where you do not want it. Every corrosion process involves at least one anodic reaction (metal dissolution) and at least one cathodic reaction (reduction of some species in the environment). The variety of corrosion types arises from the different ways anodes and cathodes are arranged on a surface.
body: All aqueous corrosion requires four elements: an anode (where metal dissolves), a cathode (where a species is reduced), an electronic path between them (the metal itself), and an ionic path (the electrolyte). Remove any one and corrosion stops. Every corrosion prevention strategy targets at least one of these four.
The anodic reaction is always metal dissolution:
The cathodic reaction depends on the environment. In acidic de-aerated solutions, it is hydrogen evolution:
In neutral or alkaline aerated solutions, it is oxygen reduction:

The oxygen reduction reaction is responsible for the majority of structural corrosion on Earth. It is the cathodic reaction that drives rusting of steel, tarnishing of copper, and atmospheric corrosion of zinc.

The simplest case. Anodes and cathodes are distributed uniformly across the surface, and the metal thins at a roughly constant rate. Unprotected carbon steel in seawater corrodes at approximately 0.1 to 0.3 mm/year. Mild steel in rural atmosphere: about 0.01 mm/year. These rates are predictable and manageable through corrosion allowances in design (specify thicker sections to account for material loss over the design life).
Corrosion rate is often expressed as a current density via Faraday's law:

where $j_{\text{corr}}$ is in A/cm$^2$, $M$ is the molar mass (g/mol), $\rho$ is density (g/cm$^3$), $n$ is the charge number, and $3.15 \times 10^7$ is the number of seconds in a year. For iron ($M = 55.85$, $n = 2$, $\rho = 7.87$): 1 $\mu$A/cm$^2$ corresponds to about 0.012 mm/year.

Connect two dissimilar metals in an electrolyte, and the more active metal (more negative potential) becomes the anode. It corrodes faster than it would alone, while the more noble metal is protected. The driving force is the potential difference between the two metals.

The classic example: steel bolts in an aluminium structure, exposed to rain. Aluminium ($E^\circ = -1.66$ V) is far more active than steel ($E^\circ \approx -0.44$ V). The aluminium around each bolt becomes an anode and corrodes preferentially, sometimes to the point of structural failure. The same physics, used deliberately, gives cathodic protection (article 10.6).

The area ratio matters enormously. A small anode connected to a large cathode produces intense local attack (all the cathodic current is supplied by dissolution of the small anode). A small cathode connected to a large anode is relatively benign. This is why stainless steel fasteners in a carbon steel plate are acceptable (small cathode, large anode), but carbon steel fasteners in a stainless steel plate are catastrophic (small anode, large cathode).

The galvanic series ranks metals and alloys by their open-circuit potential in a specific environment (usually seawater). It differs from the standard electrochemical series because it accounts for the effect of passive films. Titanium and stainless steel 316 sit near the noble end, despite their thermodynamically active base metals, because their passive films shift the practical potential positive. Always use the galvanic series for the actual service environment, not the textbook standard potentials.

Pitting is localised attack that produces small holes in an otherwise intact surface. It is insidious because the overall mass loss is tiny, but the local penetration can be rapid (mm/year at the pit base) and unpredictable. Pitting causes more structural failures than uniform corrosion.

The mechanism involves breakdown of the passive film, usually by chloride ions. Cl$^-$ ions are small, mobile, and competitive with OH$^-$ for adsorption sites on the oxide surface. Above a critical potential (the pitting potential $E_{\text{pit}}$), chloride penetrates the passive film at a defect site (an inclusion, a scratch, a grain boundary). The exposed metal dissolves rapidly, producing M$^{n+}$ ions. Hydrolysis of these ions ($\text{M}^{n+} + n\text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{M(OH)}_n + n\text{H}^+$) lowers the local pH inside the pit, further destabilising the passive film and accelerating dissolution. The pit becomes a self-sustaining, autocatalytic micro-cell.

For austenitic stainless steels, the pitting resistance equivalent number (PREN) ranks alloy resistance: $\text{PREN} = \%\text{Cr} + 3.3 \times \%\text{Mo} + 16 \times \%\text{N}$. Type 304 (18Cr-8Ni) has PREN $\approx$ 18. Type 316 (17Cr-12Ni-2.5Mo) has PREN $\approx$ 25. Super-duplex steels (25Cr-7Ni-4Mo-0.3N) reach PREN $>$ 40. A PREN above 40 is generally considered resistant to pitting in seawater.

Any geometry that creates a stagnant volume of electrolyte, too narrow for convection to refresh, is a crevice: a flange joint, a gasket, a deposit of marine fouling on a hull. Inside the crevice, dissolved oxygen is consumed by the cathodic reaction but cannot be replenished. The cathodic reaction shifts to the open surface outside the crevice, and the crevice interior becomes a net anode. Metal ions accumulate, hydrolysis lowers the pH (to as low as pH 1-2 in some cases), and chloride ions migrate in to maintain electroneutrality. The result is an aggressive micro-environment inside the crevice.

Crevice corrosion attacks many of the same alloys as pitting, and for the same reason: breakdown of the passive film in an acidified, chloride-enriched environment. The critical difference is that crevice corrosion starts at a lower potential than pitting because the geometry pre-concentrates the aggressive chemistry. An alloy that resists pitting in open seawater may still fail by crevice corrosion under a gasket.

Preferential attack along grain boundaries. The most common cause is sensitisation of austenitic stainless steel. When a steel containing 18% Cr is held at 500-800 $^\circ$C (for example, in the heat-affected zone of a weld), carbon diffuses to grain boundaries and forms Cr$_{23}$C$_6$ carbides. This depletes chromium from a narrow zone adjacent to each boundary, dropping the local Cr content below the 12% minimum needed to maintain the passive film. The depleted zone corrodes preferentially.

Solutions: use low-carbon grades (304L, 316L, with C $<$ 0.03%) so there is not enough carbon to form chromium carbides, or use stabilised grades (321 with Ti, 347 with Nb) where the stabilising element preferentially forms carbides, leaving chromium in solution. Solution annealing at 1050-1100 $^\circ$C followed by rapid cooling redissolves any existing carbides.

The combined action of a static tensile stress and a specific corrosive environment produces cracking at stress levels well below the yield strength. SCC requires three simultaneous conditions: a susceptible material, a specific environment, and a tensile stress. Remove any one and cracking does not occur.

Classic systems: austenitic stainless steel in hot chloride solutions (above 60 $^\circ$C, $[\text{Cl}^-] > 10$ ppm), brass in ammonia (season cracking, first observed in brass cartridge cases stored in horse stables), high-strength aluminium alloys (7xxx series) in moist air, and high-strength steels in hydrogen-containing environments (hydrogen embrittlement, which is mechanistically related).

Cracks propagate by a combination of anodic dissolution at the crack tip (where the passive film is ruptured by strain) and mechanical fracture of the ligament behind the crack. Crack growth rates range from $10^{-10}$ to $10^{-6}$ m/s, with catastrophic failure arriving without warning.

Fluid flow removes the protective corrosion product layer, exposing fresh metal to the environment. The corrosion rate increases with flow velocity. Copper alloy condenser tubes in power stations, carrying seawater at 2-3 m/s, suffer erosion-corrosion at tube entries and bends where turbulence is highest. The critical flow velocity for 90-10 Cu-Ni (a common condenser alloy) in seawater is about 3.5 m/s. Above this, the protective Cu$_2$O film cannot reform fast enough and corrosion rates increase sharply.

Cavitation is an extreme form: collapsing vapour bubbles generate local pressures of hundreds of MPa, physically destroying the oxide film and deforming the underlying metal. Ship propellers, pump impellers, and hydraulic turbines all suffer cavitation damage.

A carbon steel pipe ($M = 55.85$ g/mol, $n = 2$, $\rho = 7.87$ g/cm$^3$) carries aerated cooling water. The measured corrosion current density is $j_{\text{corr}} = 5$ $\mu$A/cm$^2$. Calculate the corrosion rate in mm/year and estimate how long a pipe with 3 mm corrosion allowance will last.

The corrosion rate is approximately 0.058 mm/year. With a 3 mm corrosion allowance, the pipe has an estimated service life of $3 / 0.058 \approx 52$ years. This is a reasonable figure for internal corrosion of unlined carbon steel in treated cooling water, consistent with typical industrial experience.

articles.title: Corrosion Prevention & Protection
articles.description: Cathodic protection, anodic protection, coatings, inhibitors, material selection, and design strategies for controlling corrosion.
articles.intro: Corrosion costs the global economy roughly 2.5 trillion USD per year (NACE International estimate, 2016). About a third of that is considered preventable with existing technology. This article covers the main strategies: shifting the potential into the immunity or passivity region, isolating the metal from the environment, and choosing the right material in the first place.
body: Shift the potential of the structure below the corrosion region on the Pourbaix diagram, into the immunity region. There are two methods.

Sacrificial anodes: Attach a more active metal to the structure. The active metal corrodes preferentially, driving the structure cathodic. For steel in seawater ($E_{\text{corr}} \approx -0.65$ V vs SHE), zinc ($E^\circ = -0.76$ V), magnesium ($E^\circ = -2.37$ V), or aluminium alloys are used. The anode must supply enough current to polarise the entire structure below approximately $-0.80$ V vs SHE.

Zinc anodes are the workhorse for marine applications. A typical zinc anode provides about 780 Ah/kg of capacity. To protect a ship hull with 5000 m$^2$ of wetted area requiring 100 mA/m$^2$, you need 500 A total. Over a 5-year dry-docking interval: $500 \times 5 \times 8760 / 780 = 28\,100$ kg of zinc. That is about 28 tonnes of sacrificial anodes, which gives a sense of the scale involved in marine corrosion engineering.

Impressed current: Use an external DC power supply to drive the structure cathodic. The anode is an inert conductor (graphite, platinised titanium, mixed-metal oxide coated titanium) that evolves oxygen rather than dissolving. This method is preferred for large structures (pipelines, offshore platforms) because the current and potential can be controlled precisely.

The target potential for cathodic protection of steel in seawater is $-0.80$ V vs Ag/AgCl (approximately $-0.59$ V vs SHE), based on the criterion that the corrosion rate is negligible at this potential. Over-protection (too negative a potential) wastes current and can cause hydrogen embrittlement of high-strength steels or disbonding of coatings by alkali generated at the surface.
Cathodic protection on the Pourbaix diagram

Cathodic protection simply moves the operating point on the Pourbaix diagram downward (lower potential) from the corrosion region into the immunity region. For iron at pH 8 (seawater), this means shifting from about $-0.5$ V to below about $-0.62$ V vs SHE, which matches the engineering criterion of $-0.80$ V vs Ag/AgCl ($-0.58$ V vs SHE) quite closely.

This sounds paradoxical: make the metal more positive to protect it? It works for metals that passivate. An external anodic current shifts the potential into the passivity region of the Pourbaix diagram, forming and maintaining a stable oxide film. Once the passive film is established, the maintaining current is tiny (microamps per m$^2$).

Anodic protection is used in concentrated sulphuric acid storage tanks (carbon steel or stainless steel), where the passive film is stable and the corrosion rate in the passive state is less than 0.01 mm/year, compared to over 10 mm/year in the active state. It is not applicable to metals that do not form a stable passive film (e.g., zinc, magnesium) or in environments containing aggressive ions that break down the film (e.g., chloride for many stainless steels).
Put something between the metal and the environment.

Organic coatings (paint): The global protective coatings market is enormous for good reason. A typical marine coating system consists of a zinc-rich primer (cathodic protection if the topcoat is scratched), an epoxy intermediate coat (barrier), and a polyurethane topcoat (UV resistance and aesthetics). Total dry film thickness: 300-500 $\mu$m. Design life: 15-25 years with maintenance.

Metallic coatings: Galvanising (hot-dip zinc coating on steel) provides both barrier protection and sacrificial cathodic protection. A typical coating thickness of 85 $\mu$m on structural steel gives a service life of 50-75 years in rural atmospheres, or 20-30 years in marine environments. The zinc corrodes preferentially at scratches and cut edges, protecting the exposed steel.

Ceramic coatings: Anodising of aluminium produces a dense, adherent Al$_2$O$_3$ film (typically 5-25 $\mu$m for architectural applications, up to 50 $\mu$m for hard anodising). Thermal barrier coatings of yttria-stabilised zirconia (YSZ) on nickel superalloy turbine blades serve primarily as thermal insulation but also protect against high-temperature oxidation.

Chemical species added to the environment that reduce the corrosion rate. Inhibitors work by adsorbing on the metal surface, blocking either the anodic reaction (anodic inhibitors), the cathodic reaction (cathodic inhibitors), or both (mixed inhibitors).

Chromates were historically the most effective corrosion inhibitors for aluminium alloys. Hexavalent chromium (CrO$_4^{2-}$) adsorbs at defect sites in the passive film and repairs them. Chromate conversion coatings provided the gold-standard corrosion protection in the aerospace industry for decades. Environmental and health regulations (REACH in the EU, RoHS) now severely restrict Cr(VI), driving a major research effort into alternatives (rare-earth inhibitors, sol-gel coatings, conducting polymers).

Phosphates and molybdates are anodic inhibitors for steel in near-neutral water. They promote the formation of a protective iron phosphate or molybdate film. Sodium molybdate at 50-200 ppm is widely used in cooling water treatment.
Filming amines form a hydrophobic barrier layer on the steel surface. They are used in steam condensate systems and in oil and gas pipelines.
The cheapest corrosion prevention is choosing the right material for the environment from the start. Some guidelines that encode the electrochemistry:
Avoid coupling dissimilar metals. If unavoidable, insulate the joint and ensure the anode area is much larger than the cathode area.
Eliminate crevices in design. Use butt welds rather than lap joints. Seal flanges. Avoid geometries that trap stagnant liquid.
Specify low-carbon or stabilised stainless steels for welded structures to prevent sensitisation.
In chloride environments, select alloys with PREN appropriate for the service conditions. PREN $>$ 40 for seawater immersion.
Provide drainage. Standing water accelerates corrosion. Structural sections should not accumulate pools.

Consider the full lifecycle: initial cost, maintenance, inspection intervals, and eventual replacement. A stainless steel system that lasts 50 years with no maintenance may be cheaper than a carbon steel system that requires painting every 5 years.

In real corrosion, the anodic and cathodic reactions are different. The metal adopts a potential, the corrosion potential $E_{\text{corr}}$, where the total anodic current equals the total cathodic current. This is the mixed potential.
The corrosion potential and corrosion rate are determined by the intersection of the anodic and cathodic polarisation curves.

Write the Butler-Volmer equation for each reaction. At the corrosion potential, $j_a(E_{\text{corr}}) = j_c(E_{\text{corr}})$. Graphically, plot $\log |j|$ vs $E$ for both reactions. The anodic curve for metal dissolution rises with increasing $E$. The cathodic curve for oxygen reduction falls with increasing $E$. They intersect at $E_{\text{corr}}$, and the current at the intersection is $j_{\text{corr}}$.

This is the Evans diagram. It shows immediately why cathodic protection works (shifting $E$ below $E_{\text{corr}}$ reduces $j_a$ exponentially), why oxygen concentration affects corrosion rate (more dissolved O$_2$ increases $j_c$, moving the intersection to higher $j_{\text{corr}}$), and why inhibitors that increase the Tafel slope reduce $j_{\text{corr}}$ even without changing $E_{\text{corr}}$ much.

A buried steel pipeline is cathodically protected with magnesium sacrificial anodes. The pipeline requires a protection current density of 20 mA/m$^2$, has an external surface area of 3000 m$^2$, and the magnesium anodes have a practical capacity of 1100 Ah/kg. How many kilograms of magnesium are consumed per year?

Approximately 480 kg of magnesium per year. Over a 20-year design life between anode replacements, that is nearly 10 tonnes of magnesium. In practice, anodes are oversized by 10-20% to account for non-uniform current distribution and anode self-corrosion. Pipeline cathodic protection systems are typically designed to a standard such as ISO 15589-1 or NACE SP0169.

articles.title: Batteries, Fuel Cells & Electrolysers
articles.description: Lithium-ion batteries, solid-state batteries, PEM fuel cells, and alkaline electrolysers: operating principles, real voltages, energy densities, and materials challenges.
articles.intro: Batteries, fuel cells, and electrolysers are electrochemical cells engineered for energy storage and conversion. The thermodynamics and kinetics developed in articles 10.1-10.3 apply directly. What distinguishes these devices from corrosion is intent: we want the electrochemical reactions to proceed, and we want them to be efficient, reversible (for rechargeable systems), and durable.
body: A battery is a galvanic cell designed to deliver electrical energy from a chemical reaction. The key performance metrics are:
Cell voltage: the potential difference between cathode and anode. Higher voltage means more energy per electron transferred.
Specific capacity (mAh/g): the charge stored per unit mass of electrode. Determined by the molar mass and the number of electrons transferred per formula unit.
Specific energy (Wh/kg): voltage times specific capacity. This is the figure that determines range in electric vehicles and flight time in drones.
Cycle life: number of charge-discharge cycles before capacity drops below 80% of the initial value.
Rate capability: how fast the battery can charge and discharge without excessive voltage loss.

The theoretical specific energy is set by thermodynamics ($\Delta G = -nFE$). The practical specific energy is always lower, reduced by overpotentials (activation, ohmic, concentration), the mass of inactive components (current collectors, separator, electrolyte, housing), and the need to avoid side reactions at extreme states of charge.

The dominant rechargeable battery technology since Sony commercialised it in 1991. The basic principle: lithium ions shuttle between two intercalation host structures. During discharge, Li$^+$ deintercalates from the graphite anode and intercalates into the cathode. During charge, the process reverses. The electrolyte (typically 1 M LiPF$_6$ in a mixture of ethylene carbonate and dimethyl carbonate) conducts Li$^+$ but is an electronic insulator.
The anode is graphite: $\text{LiC}_6 \rightleftharpoons \text{Li}^+ + e^- + \text{C}_6$. The equilibrium potential is about 0.1 V vs Li/Li$^+$. Theoretical capacity: 372 mAh/g.
The cathode determines the cell chemistry. Three families dominate:

LiCoO$_2$ (LCO): the original cathode material. Layered structure (R$\bar{3}$m). Practical capacity: 140 mAh/g (only about half the lithium can be reversibly extracted). Average voltage: 3.8 V vs Li/Li$^+$. Used in consumer electronics. Cobalt is expensive (roughly $30/kg in 2024) and ethically problematic (most cobalt is mined in the DRC).

LiFePO$_4$ (LFP): olivine structure (Pnma). Capacity: 170 mAh/g. Voltage: 3.4 V vs Li/Li$^+$, with a very flat charge-discharge plateau (two-phase reaction). Excellent cycle life ($>$3000 cycles to 80% capacity), no cobalt or nickel, thermally stable. Lower energy density than nickel-rich cathodes. Used in stationary storage and increasingly in EVs (Tesla, BYD).

LiNi$_x$Mn$_y$Co$_z$O$_2$ (NMC): layered structure. NMC811 (80% Ni, 10% Mn, 10% Co) provides about 200 mAh/g at 3.7 V. Higher energy density than LFP, but less thermally stable and shorter cycle life. Dominates the EV market where range is the priority.
LFP/graphite: 150-180 Wh/kg at the cell level
NMC811/graphite: 250-300 Wh/kg at the cell level

At the pack level, add 30-40% mass for the battery management system, cooling, wiring, and structural casing. A 75 kWh Tesla Model 3 pack with NMC cells weighs about 480 kg, giving a pack-level energy density of approximately 156 Wh/kg.
Voltage losses in a real cell
The open-circuit voltage (OCV) of an NMC811/graphite cell is about 4.2 V at full charge and 2.5 V at full discharge. Under load, the terminal voltage drops:

At 1C discharge rate (full capacity in one hour), the total overpotential is typically 0.1-0.3 V. At 5C (fast discharge), it can exceed 0.5 V. These losses appear as heat, which is why fast charging requires thermal management.

On the first charge cycle, the organic electrolyte decomposes at the graphite surface (below about 0.8 V vs Li/Li$^+$) and forms a thin ($\sim$20 nm), ionically conducting, electronically insulating film called the SEI. This film is essential: without it, the electrolyte would continuously decompose. But forming it consumes lithium irreversibly, causing 5-10% first-cycle capacity loss. SEI growth continues slowly over the life of the cell and is the primary aging mechanism in well-designed Li-ion batteries.

Replace the flammable liquid electrolyte with a solid ionic conductor. The potential advantages: non-flammable, enabling lithium metal anodes (which are unstable against liquid electrolytes), and therefore higher energy density.

A lithium metal anode has a theoretical capacity of 3860 mAh/g, more than ten times that of graphite. Combined with a high-voltage cathode, solid-state cells could reach 400-500 Wh/kg at the cell level. The challenge is making a solid electrolyte with sufficient ionic conductivity.

Oxide ceramics: Li$_7$La$_3$Zr$_2$O$_{12}$ (LLZO, garnet structure). Ionic conductivity: $\sim$1 mS/cm at 25 $^\circ$C. Electrochemically stable to $>$5 V vs Li/Li$^+$. Hard and brittle, requiring high-temperature sintering ($>$1000 $^\circ$C) and careful interface engineering to achieve good contact with the electrodes.

Sulphide glasses: Li$_6$PS$_5$Cl (argyrodite). Ionic conductivity: 1-5 mS/cm at 25 $^\circ$C, comparable to liquid electrolytes. Soft and deformable (good electrode contact), but reactive with moisture (produces H$_2$S) and with lithium metal. Narrow electrochemical stability window ($\sim$1.7-2.1 V vs Li/Li$^+$) requiring protective coatings.

Polymer electrolytes: PEO-LiTFSI. Ionic conductivity: $\sim$0.01 mS/cm at 25 $^\circ$C, but $\sim$1 mS/cm at 80 $^\circ$C. Used in the Bollore Bluecar (Paris car-sharing) at elevated temperature. Simple processing, but low room-temperature conductivity limits applications.

The key unsolved problem is the lithium metal-electrolyte interface. Lithium dendrites grow through solid electrolytes along grain boundaries and pores, eventually short-circuiting the cell. Current density limits for dendrite-free cycling in LLZO are around 0.5-1.0 mA/cm$^2$ at room temperature, well below the 3-5 mA/cm$^2$ needed for fast-charging EVs.
A proton exchange membrane (PEM) fuel cell converts hydrogen and oxygen to water, generating electricity directly. The overall reaction is:
This is the maximum voltage at 298 K and 1 bar. In practice, a PEM fuel cell operates at 0.6-0.8 V per cell under load. The 0.4-0.6 V of losses come from:

Activation overpotential: dominated by the sluggish oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) at the cathode. The exchange current density for ORR on platinum is only $\sim$$10^{-9}$ A/cm$^2$ (per geometric area), requiring $\sim$0.3-0.4 V of overpotential to drive useful current densities (0.5-1.5 A/cm$^2$).
Ohmic losses: ionic resistance through the Nafion membrane (typically 25-50 $\mu$m thick) and electronic contact resistance. Nafion 211 has a conductivity of about 0.1 S/cm when fully hydrated.
Mass transport: at high current densities ($>$1.5 A/cm$^2$), liquid water produced at the cathode can flood the gas diffusion layer, blocking oxygen access.

The membrane electrode assembly (MEA) uses platinum or platinum-alloy catalysts on carbon supports. Typical Pt loading: 0.1 mg/cm$^2$ at the anode (hydrogen oxidation is fast) and 0.3-0.4 mg/cm$^2$ at the cathode. Total Pt loading per kW of power: roughly 0.3-0.5 g$_{\text{Pt}}$/kW for current commercial systems. Platinum costs about $30/g (2024), so catalyst cost is $10-15/kW, a significant but no longer dominant fraction of the stack cost.
PEM fuel cell stacks in vehicles (Toyota Mirai, Hyundai Nexo) produce 80-130 kW from 300-400 individual cells in series, achieving system efficiencies of 50-60% (HHV basis) at rated power.

An electrolyser is a fuel cell run in reverse: electrical energy drives the splitting of water into hydrogen and oxygen. The minimum (thermodynamic) voltage is 1.229 V at 298 K (the thermoneutral voltage, accounting for the entropy term, is 1.481 V).
In an alkaline electrolyser, the reactions are:

The electrolyte is 25-30 wt% KOH (high conductivity: $\sim$0.6 S/cm at 80 $^\circ$C). Operating temperature: 60-90 $^\circ$C. Electrodes: nickel (anode) and nickel with catalytic coatings such as Raney nickel (cathode). The separator is a porous diaphragm (traditionally asbestos, now replaced by Zirfon, a composite of ZrO$_2$ and polysulphone).

Practical cell voltages: 1.8-2.1 V at typical current densities of 200-400 mA/cm$^2$. The voltage efficiency is $E_{\text{thermo}}/V_{\text{cell}} = 1.481/1.9 \approx 78\%$. System-level efficiency including pumps, heat management, and gas purification: 60-70% (LHV basis).

A commercial alkaline electrolyser stack produces hydrogen at roughly 4.5-5.5 kWh per Nm$^3$ of H$_2$ (the thermodynamic minimum is 3.0 kWh/Nm$^3$). At scale (10 MW+), capital costs are $500-1000/kW, with the stack accounting for about 50% and the balance of plant the remainder. PEM electrolysers operate at higher current densities (1-3 A/cm$^2$) and respond faster to variable input power (useful for coupling to renewables), but they require iridium and platinum catalysts and cost roughly 1.5-2x more per kW.
Electrochemical energy storage: the materials perspective
The theoretical specific energy of an electrochemical couple is set by the cell voltage and the specific capacities of both electrodes.
For a cell with cathode capacity $Q_c$ (mAh/g), anode capacity $Q_a$ (mAh/g), and average voltage $V_{\text{avg}}$ (V), the theoretical specific energy based on active materials only is:
The practical cell-level value of 250-300 Wh/kg represents about 55-65% of this theoretical figure. The gap is due to inactive materials and incomplete utilisation of the electrode capacity.

The quest for higher energy density drives research into new chemistries. Lithium-sulphur (Li-S) has a theoretical specific energy of 2600 Wh/kg ($E \approx 2.1$ V, S capacity = 1675 mAh/g), but practical cells achieve only 300-400 Wh/kg due to polysulphide dissolution, volume expansion (80% for sulphur), and poor cycle life. Lithium-air (Li-O$_2$) has the highest theoretical energy density of any battery chemistry (3500 Wh/kg), but remains a laboratory curiosity due to irreversibility of the Li$_2$O$_2$ discharge product and contamination by CO$_2$ and H$_2$O.

Sodium-ion batteries are the nearest-term alternative to Li-ion. They use abundant sodium instead of lithium (Na: 23,000 ppm in the Earth's crust vs Li: 20 ppm), with hard carbon anodes and layered oxide or Prussian blue analogue cathodes. Cell voltage: 3.0-3.3 V. Energy density: 140-160 Wh/kg at the cell level. Already commercialised by CATL and HiNa, primarily for stationary storage where cost per kWh matters more than mass.

Chemical bonds store far more energy per unit mass than any other mechanism accessible at ambient conditions. The specific energy of petrol is about 12,000 Wh/kg (of which a combustion engine extracts $\sim$3000 Wh/kg as useful work). The best Li-ion cells deliver 300 Wh/kg. The gap has narrowed by a factor of ten since lead-acid (35 Wh/kg), but physics imposes limits: the electrochemical series sets the maximum voltage per electron, and the periodic table sets the minimum mass per mole of charge carrier. Future improvements will be incremental, not transformative.

A PEM electrolyser operates at a cell voltage of 1.85 V and a current density of 2 A/cm$^2$. Calculate: (a) the voltage efficiency, (b) the hydrogen production rate per cm$^2$ of electrode, and (c) the energy consumption per kg of H$_2$.
(b) Hydrogen production rate per cm$^2$ (using Faraday's law, $n = 2$ for H$_2$):

At the thermodynamic minimum (1.229 V), the energy would be 32.9 kWh/kg. The 49.2 kWh/kg reflects the 80% voltage efficiency. A state-of-the-art PEM electrolyser operating at this voltage and current density is competitive with alkaline technology on efficiency but offers faster dynamic response.
